analysis.one_liner: Sets 18-year terms for future Supreme Court justices with a new appointment every two years.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2025 with nine House members' support and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which has taken no action on it since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the President to nominate a Supreme Court justice every two years, with each justice serving an active 18-year term before stepping into a backup role. Justices already on the Court when the bill passes would be exempt. If the Senate sits on a nomination for more than 120 days, the nominee would be seated without Senate approval. The bill went to the House Judiciary Committee and has not moved since.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people would get a Supreme Court that turns over on a predictable schedule instead of changing composition only when a justice dies or retires at a politically convenient moment. Future presidents of either party would each get appointments at regular intervals, reducing the winner-take-all fights that occur when seats open up unexpectedly. Justices after 18 years could still hear cases as senior justices if assigned.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Voters wanting a regularly refreshed Supreme Court

how_it_helps.text: The President would nominate one justice during the first and third years after each presidential election, making appointments a regular feature of every administration rather than a rare event [S2][S3].

After 18 years of service, a justice would move to 'senior justice' status and could still be assigned cases, including filling temporary vacancies, so the Court would keep experienced hands while guaranteeing turnover [S2][S3].

If the Senate does not act on a Supreme Court nominee within 120 days, the nominee would be seated without Senate confirmation, closing the loophole used in recent decades when Senate majorities held seats open [S2][S3].

If a seat opens unexpectedly through death, disability, or removal, the most recently retired senior justice would fill in until a new appointment is made, so the Court would keep nine active members [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The Senate would lose its ability to delay or block Supreme Court nominees indefinitely, and the constitutional question is real: the Constitution says justices hold office 'during good Behaviour,' so a term-limit law enacted by ordinary legislation would almost certainly be challenged in court, with many scholars arguing it requires a constitutional amendment. Incumbent justices are exempt, so the current Court's composition would not change unless a new justice is seated under the new schedule.

drawbacks.text: Justices already on the Court when the bill passes are explicitly exempt: they would not count toward the active panel of nine and would not be required to retire [S2][S3]. That means the current Court could keep its seats for decades while the new limits apply only to future appointees, and the drafting leaves unclear whether those grandfathered justices would still vote alongside the rotating panel of nine.

Article III of the Constitution gives justices their seats 'during good Behaviour,' and most legal scholars read that as lifetime tenure that ordinary legislation cannot cut short. A court challenge to this law would be likely, and the same justices whose terms it would limit could end up ruling on its validity. The Senate's 120-day confirmation deadline also removes a check that lets the upper chamber scrutinize nominees.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Regular appointments and a hard confirmation deadline would fix two real problems: lifetime tenure that lets a single generation of appointees shape the law for decades, and Senate delays that have left seats open for political gain. But the exemption for current justices means the Court would not actually change for many years, and the constitutional roadblock means the bill might never take effect even if passed. As a statement of principle with a built-in grandfather clause, it is more symbolic than transformative.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in February 2025 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a committee vote, or floor action ever since.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the Supreme Court Term Limits and Regular Appointments Act on February 6, 2025 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on the Judiciary, its only committee assignment [S5].
Eight additional House Democrats cosponsored the bill; all nine supporters are Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral [S5].
Congress remains in session through January 2027, so the bill technically remains alive in committee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Incumbent Supreme Court justices and the current Senate majority are better off so far, because the bill would have curtailed both lifetime tenure and Senate confirmation leverage, and neither has had to give anything up while it sits untouched in committee.

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters are Democrats; the bill has no Republican cosponsors, and it sits in a committee controlled by Republicans who have not acted on it.

industries.note: The bill exempts every justice appointed before enactment: they are not required to retire and are not counted toward the active panel of nine. The current Court keeps its seats indefinitely while the new 18-year terms bind only future appointees, so the bill regulates the institution without touching the people who hold power under the old rules.

Presidents would gain a guaranteed seat appointment in years one and three of each term, and a 120-day deadline that prevents the Senate from holding nominations open indefinitely. The Senate would lose its ability to stall nominees, shifting appointment power toward the White House.

analysis.trajectory: This bill sits with no cosponsors from the majority party, no committee hearing, and a constitutional design question that most scholars say requires a constitutional amendment rather than a statute. Term-limit proposals like this have been introduced repeatedly in past Congresses and have never reached a floor vote. The realistic path is that it stays in the Judiciary Committee until the 119th Congress ends in January 2027, unless the politics of Supreme Court reform change dramatically.
